I.        Introduction
           4K Land and Cattle Company (“4K Land”) respectfully submits this Initial Brief and urges
the Administrative Law Judges and the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“PUC” OR
“Commission”) to reject any route that uses Links M12, M11, K52, and K51 and to instead select
a Northern Corridor route that follows existing civic and industrial infrastructure, including Routes
416, 410, 392, 402, 391, 589, 592, 74, 93, and 100.
           The Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV line, spanning approximately 214-244 miles at
an estimated cost exceeding $1.6 billion, represents one of the largest transmission projects ever
undertaken in Texas, and the burden it places on landowners is correspondingly large. 1 As a
preliminary matter, the Application offers only subjective and selectively applied references,
drawn from an incomplete catalog of data, with no foundational analysis measured against the
standards of transmission-line routing or against fifty years of progress in environmental

         4K Land is the owner of approximately 100,000 acres of land in Mason, McCulloch, and

operation encompassing commercial cattle production, hay and forage production, agricultural
farming, comprehensive wildlife management, hunting leases and guided hunts, ecotourism, and
equestrian activities. 4 The proposed 765-kV transmission line would inflict substantial, permanent
harm on the property. 5

codified as the Electric Power Research Institute–Georgia Transmission Corporation (“EPRI-
GTC”) methodology for overhead transmission line siting — has measured the Application not
against a preference of his own or that of 4K Land, but against the ordinary requirements of a
nationally-recognized defensible siting method. 6 That a project of this magnitude arrives with 122

minimal thresholds and offered nothing of consequence, leaving to the Commission the very
comparative judgment the Applicants were obligated to perform.
         Stated plainly, this record now asks the Commission to certify a route where evidence
shows the following: a process that seated affected landowners and the public in the back seat
rather than at the table; a record left incomplete on the very factors the regulatory framework
makes central; and a recommendation that rests on no consistent basis, because the statute was

the 122 filed routes, while Northern Corridor routes, including Routes 416, 410, and 392, rank first
(tie), first (tie), and third “least worst” route, respectively. 7 The testimony of J. Luther King, Jr.,

III.   Statutory and Regulatory Transmission Routing Framework

        a. PURA and Commission Rules

        PURA § 37.056(c) requires the Commission to grant a certificate of convenience and
necessity after considering, among other factors: (A) community values; (B) recreational and park
areas; (C) historical and aesthetic values; (D) environmental integrity; (E) the probable
improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers; and (F) the need for extending
transmission service where existing or projected electrical loads will be underserved. These factors
are mandatory; the Commission must weigh them when evaluating routes.
        The Commission’s Substantive Rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), requires that a new
transmission line “must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected
community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise.” The rule further
requires consideration of whether routes: (i) parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way
for electric facilities; (ii) parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-of-way; (iii) parallel
property lines or other natural or cultural features; and (iv) conform with the policy of prudent
avoidance.

        b. This Framework Demands an Application of All PURA and Commission Criteria

        Together, PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) enumerate a number of
codified criteria. The Applicants’ record operatively addresses only two of these factors:
engineering constraints and costs. 15 The remaining factors, including community values,
recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, moderation of impact on the affected
community and landowners, and parallelism with compatible rights-of-way, are either unweighted,
unquantified, or entirely unanalyzed. 16
        The Legislature named the right things—PURA § 37.056 directs the Commission to
consider these factors. The factors are co-equal and bound. For example, a spring rising on private

        c. The Commission May Select Any Filed Route
        SOAH Order No. 1 directs that the Applicants’ preferred route carries no special weight
and that all alternatives are equally before the Commission.17 The Applicants themselves admit
that all 122 filed routes are acceptable and that they do not oppose the selection of any filed route,
including routes in the Northern Corridor using Link U6. 18 Because the Applicants concede that
every filed route is acceptable and decline to defend Route 894 as uniquely required, the
Commission may select a Northern Corridor route without overriding any preference the
Applicants are entitled to assert—leaving the comparative judgment squarely within the
Commission’s unbounded discretion to apply the full statutory and regulatory criteria.
IV.    The Applicants Did Not Present a Transparent Routing Methodology
        a. The Applicants’ Process Functions as a “Black Box”
        The central deficiency in the Applicants’ filing is that it lacks a methodology—the
governing framework that would allow a reviewing authority to determine how the work was done
and whether it can be reproduced.
        Mr. Scott identified six minimum constitutive elements of a defensible methodology: (1) a
study area derived from base terrain analysis; (2) transparent weight derivation subjected to
sensitivity testing; (3) multi-perspective decomposition; (4) an intermediate surface audit trail; (5)
reproducibility; and (6) a canonical data inventory with source provenance. 19 Against every one
of these elements, the Applicants’ record fails. The Applicants confirmed in response to 4K Land’s
RFI 1-4 that they “did not assign weights to factors or sub-factors in their routing analysis,” and
in response to RFI 1-5 that they “did not perform” any sensitivity analysis to test Route 894’s
stability under alternative weighting schemes. 20
        Thus, the Applicants’ process functions, in practical terms, as a black box: it produces
outputs — 122 routes and a “best meets” designation — without disclosing a disciplined,

        c. Mr. Scott’s Methodology Is Transparent, Reproducible, and Standards-Compliant

         In contrast to the Applicants’ opaque process, Mr. Scott applied the EPRI-GTC
methodology—a national standard for overhead electric transmission line siting adapted to Texas
statute in four synthesis perspectives. 40 Mr. Scott was instrumental in developing the original

process does not cure the flaw.

VI.    The Applicants’ Inverted the Analytical Process

adequate routing analysis, data and public engagement precede and shape the routes. Here, the

have produced them came after. Mr. Scott testified that the public meetings held by the Applicants
asked landowners “to respond to a set of predetermined routes rather than to contribute values that
would shape the analysis producing those routes,” which he described as “the operational meaning
of notification masquerading as participation — a structured opportunity to react, presented as
though it were a structured opportunity to shape.” 53

III.    Statutory and Regulatory Transmission Routing Framework

         a. PURA and Commission Rules

        PURA § 37.056(c) requires the Commission to grant a certificate of convenience and
necessity after considering, among other factors: (A) community values; (B) recreational and park
areas; (C) historical and aesthetic values; (D) environmental integrity; (E) the probable
improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers; and (F) the need for extending
transmission service where existing or proj ected electrical loads will be underserved. These factors
are mandatory; the Commission must weigh them when evaluating routes.
         The Commission' s Substantive Rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), requires that a new
transmission line "must be routed to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected
community and landowners unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise." The rule further
requires consideration of whether routes: (i) parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way
for electric facilities; (ii) parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-of-way; (iii) parallel
property lines or other natural or cultural features; and (iv) conform with the policy of prudent
avoidance.

codified criteria. The Applicants' record operatively addresses only two of these factors:
engineering constraints and costs. 15 The remaining factors, including community values,
recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, moderation of impact on the affected
community and landowners, and parallelism with compatible rights-of-way, are either unweighted,
unquantified, or entirely unanalyzed. 16
